table.caption: Crude birth and death rates, per 1,000 people per year, in one country (invented data for practice)

items.q: In which stage of the model is the gap between the birth rate and the death rate widest?
options: Stage 2, transitional
Stage 1, preindustrial
Stage 3, industrial
Stage 4, postindustrial

why.correct: The widest gap means the fastest natural increase.
options: Right: the death rate has fallen but the birth rate is still near 40, so the shaded gap is widest.
Both rates are high and close together; growth is slow.
The birth rate is falling, so the gap is narrowing.
Both rates are low and close together.

items.q: According to the model, what change marks the start of stage 3?
options: The death rate begins to fall
The birth rate begins to fall steeply
Both rates rise together
The death rate rises above the birth rate

why.correct: Stage 2 is the falling death rate; stage 3 is the falling birth rate.
options: The death rate falls in stage 2, before stage 3.
Right: in stage 3 the birth rate drops toward the death rate.
Neither rate rises in the model.
That does not happen in stage 3.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the falling death rate in stage 2?
options: Women having fewer children
More people moving to other countries
Clean water, vaccines and more reliable food
An older population with many more retirees

why.correct: Death rates fall first because public health spreads faster than changes in family size.
options: That lowers the birth rate, which happens later, in stage 3.
Migration does not change the crude death rate in the model.
Right: these cut deaths from disease and hunger, especially among children.
An older population would raise the death rate, not lower it.

items.q: Near the middle of stage 2, the model shows a crude birth rate of about 40 and a crude death rate of about 21. What is the rate of natural increase, in percent?

mistakes.why: That is the gap per 1,000 people. Divide by 10 for a percent.
You divided by 100. Divide the difference by 10.

items.q: In the table, between which two years did the country’s death rate fall the most?

why.correct: Subtract each pair of death rates and compare.
options: From 20 to 12 is a drop of 8.
From 12 to 9 is a drop of 3.
From 9 to 10 is a small rise.
Right: from 34 to 20, a drop of 14 per 1,000.

items.q: What was the country’s rate of natural increase in 1910, in percent?

mistakes.why: That is the gap per 1,000. Divide by 10 for a percent.

items.q: Using the 1910 rate of natural increase of 1.7%, write the setup for the country’s doubling time, then give the answer, rounded to the nearest year.

mistakes.why: That divides by 17. Use 1.7: 70 / 1.7 is about 41 years.
That divides by 0.017. Use the rate in percent.
Use the growth rate in percent, 1.7, not the gap per 1,000 (17).
Use the rate in percent (1.7), not as a decimal.

items.q: Which stage of the demographic transition best fits the country in 2020?
options: Stage 4
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Right: both rates are low and equal at 10, so natural increase is zero.
Stage 1 has high birth and death rates; these are low.
Stage 2 has a high birth rate; 10 is low.
In stage 3 the birth rate is still well above the death rate.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the two rates changed from 1870 to 2020?
options: The birth rate fell first, and the death rate fell later
The death rate fell first, and the birth rate fell later
Both rates fell at the same time and by the same amount
Both rates rose over the 150 years

why.correct: This order, deaths first and births later, is the core of the demographic transition.
options: Births stayed near 37 to 38 until 1910, while deaths had already fallen.
Right: by 1910 deaths had fallen to 20 while births were still 37; births dropped mainly after 1950.
Deaths fell early, births later, and by different amounts.
Both fell overall.

items.q: Which stage of the demographic transition has high birth rates, high death rates and slow population growth?
options: Transitional
Industrial
Preindustrial
Postindustrial
In the transitional stage the death rate has fallen, so growth is fast.
In the industrial stage the birth rate is falling.
Right: both rates are high, so the gap and the growth are small.
In the postindustrial stage both rates are low.

items.q: Which changes usually help move a country from stage 2 to stage 3? Select all that apply.
options: More girls stay in school and more women work for pay
Infant mortality rises, so families need more births
Most families stay on farms where children work
Clean water first reaches villages

why.correct: Stage 3 is driven by the falling birth rate: schooling, paid work, low infant mortality and family planning all lower it.
options: Right: both lower the birth rate.
Rising infant mortality pushes fertility up, the opposite of stage 3.
Farm work by children keeps the birth rate high.
Clean water lowers the death rate, which is the change into stage 2.

items.q: Explain why a country’s population grows fastest in stage 2 of the demographic transition.

why.correct: Deaths fall, births stay high, the gap widens, growth peaks.

cause.label: Death rate
options: the death rate falls because of clean water, vaccines and better food
the death rate rises because of disease
the death rate stays at its stage 1 level

why.1: Deaths fall in stage 2, not rise.
why.2: The fall in the death rate is what starts stage 2.

effect.label: Birth rate
options: the birth rate stays high
the birth rate falls just as fast
the birth rate drops below the death rate

why.1: If births fell as fast, the gap would not widen.
why.2: Births stay far above deaths in stage 2.

mechanism.label: Result
options: the gap between births and deaths, and so the growth rate, is at its largest
the population shrinks
births and deaths balance out

why.1: With births far above deaths, the population grows.
why.2: Balance comes in stages 1 and 4, not 2.

specific.model: In stage 2, the death rate falls because of clean water, vaccines and better food while the birth rate stays high, so the gap between births and deaths, and so the growth rate, is at its largest.

items.q: Which age structure diagram is typical of a country in stage 2 of the demographic transition?
options: A column with equal bars up to old age
A base narrower than the middle
A top that is much wider than the base
A wide base narrowing fast with age

why.correct: Stage 2: high births and falling child deaths make a very wide base.
options: That fits stage 4.
That fits late stage 4, a declining population.
That is not typical of any stage.
Right: many children are surviving while birth rates are still high.

items.q: A country in stage 4 has a crude birth rate of 8 and a crude death rate of 11. What is most likely true of it?
options: It will shrink unless people move in
Its population grows fast from natural increase
It is in the preindustrial stage, with high rates
It has a very wide base on its pyramid

why.correct: Some countries go past stage 4 into decline, when births fall below deaths.
options: Right: natural increase is (8 - 11) / 10 = -0.3% a year.
Deaths outnumber births, so natural increase is negative.
Preindustrial rates are both high, near 40; 8 and 11 are low, which fits stage 4.
Few births mean a narrow base.

items.q: Why do some scientists say the model may not fit every developing country today?
options: Most countries today are already in stage 4
Some lowered death rates fast but stay poor, so births stay high
Death rates rise in the transitional stage everywhere
The model has two stages, which is too few

why.correct: The model describes a common pattern, not a law every country must follow.
options: Many countries are still in stages 2 and 3.
Right: the model was built from countries that developed economically as their rates fell; not every country follows that path.
Death rates fall in stage 2.
The model has four stages.
